content: Fortified foods containing vitamin A and zinc, when prepared according to WHO specifications, are strongly recommended, although the evidence supporting this is of very low quality. For HIV-infected children with severe acute malnutrition who experience persistent diarrhea unresponsive to standard management, it is essential to investigate for carbohydrate intolerance and infectious causes. These conditions may require alternative management strategies, such as adjustments in fluid and feeding regimens or the use of antibiotics. This recommendation is also supported by very low-quality evidence. Infants under six months of age with severe acute malnutrition and complicating factors should be admitted for inpatient care. These factors include serious clinical conditions or medical complications similar to those seen in older children with severe acute malnutrition, recent weight loss or failure to gain weight, persistent diarrhea lasting more than 14 days, ineffective feeding (observed for 15–20 minutes in a supervised setting), any pitting edema, or adverse social circumstances such as caregiver disability or depression. These recommendations are strongly supported, though the evidence quality is very low. Infants under six months with severe acute malnutrition should receive the same general medical care as older children with the condition. This includes parenteral antibiotics for possible sepsis and appropriate treatment for other medical complications such as tuberculosis, HIV, surgical conditions, or disabilities. For infants not admitted to inpatient care, a course of weight-adjusted broad-spectrum oral antibiotics, such as amoxicillin, is recommended. These recommendations are strongly supported, though the evidence quality is very low. Feeding strategies for infants under six months with severe acute malnutrition should prioritize establishing or re-establishing effective exclusive breastfeeding by the mother or caregiver. If breastfeeding is not possible, support should be provided to re-lactate, or wet nursing should be encouraged. Supplementary feeding may also be necessary. For infants without edema, expressed breast milk is preferred, but if unavailable, commercial infant formula or therapeutic diets like F-75 or diluted F-100 can be used. For infants with edema, infant formula or F-75 should be given as a supplement to breast milk. Undiluted F-100 should never be used due to its high renal solute load and risk of hypernatremic dehydration. Mothers or caregivers of infants with severe acute malnutrition should have their physical and mental health assessed, with appropriate treatment or support provided. Infants admitted to inpatient care can be transferred to outpatient care when all medical complications, including edema, are resolved, the infant has a good appetite, is clinically well and alert, and demonstrates adequate weight gain. Immunizations and routine interventions should also be checked, and caregivers should be linked to community-based follow-up and support. Infants can be discharged from all care when they are breastfeeding effectively or feeding well with replacement feeds, have adequate weight gain, and achieve a weight-for-length Z-score of ≥ -2. For caregivers who decline admission for assessment and treatment, counseling and support for optimal infant and young child feeding should be provided. Weekly monitoring of the infant’s weight gain is essential, and if the infant fails to gain weight or loses weight despite breastfeeding support, they should be referred to inpatient care. Caregiver health should also be assessed, and relevant support or treatment should be offered. Research priorities have been identified to address gaps in evidence related to the management of severe acute malnutrition in infants and children. These include improving clinical, epidemiological, and operational knowledge, particularly in areas such as therapeutic feeding, fluid management, and the management of HIV-infected children with severe acute malnutrition. The guideline aims to provide evidence-based recommendations to improve the care of malnourished children, reduce child mortality, and support global nutrition targets, including reducing stunting and wasting in children under five years of age.
